To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the East Indian Railway Company strike of 1921-1922 is an important moment in the history of worker politics in India and in the history of Indian nationalism.

the East Indian Railway Company strike of 1920-1922 was the first large-scale industrial action in British India, that it was a strike of unprecedented scale and intensity, that it involved a large number of workers, that it was led by the workers, that it lasted for a long time, that it involved the use of violence and that it was a success.
the strike of 1921-1922, which was a response to the alleged assault on a woman, was a significant event that exposed the limits of both colonialism and political nationalism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the strike, colonialism, nationalism and the state.

the ways in which workers, through the strike, asserted their rights and resisted the colonial state and its nationalist representatives. The EIR strike, I will argue is exemplary in this respect, and thus, is an ideal case

understanding the ways in which the EIR strike was a site of contestation over the terms of citizenship and the limits of colonialism, and how this contestation was enabled by the trans colonial context of interwar politics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the EIR strike of 1921-22 was a watershed moment in worker resistance, which was not only an exemplary moment in the history of Indian labour politics, but also a moment of trans colonial significance in the making of worker politics.

the strike of 1920-1922 was a moment of radical transformation in the politics of the working class in the colonial period, which had a profound impact on the politics of the interwar and postwar years.
the EIR strike was a moment of resistance that was both anti colonial and anti nationalist.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the strike was a critical event in the history of Indian workers and the history of the Indian nation.

the East Indian Railway workers' strike of 1921-2, in the face of a nationalist and colonial state, was a moment when workers, as subjects of empire, asserted a right to citizenship, and a right to be heard, by the colonial state.

the strike was a moment in which the workers, through the strike, articulated a vision of rights and resistance that was distinct from both colonialism and nationalism, and that this moment was not an aberration but was part of a broader pattern of resistance in the interwar period.
The main takeaway from our work is that
workers were not merely the objects of political nationalism but also its subjects, who actively shaped the political landscape.
workers' struggles are not simply a reaction to the colonial state or nationalist politics.

the strike was a moment of political possibility for Indian workers, and that this moment was made possible by the interplay between Indian and colonial discourses of governance, and the transnational circulation of labour and political ideas.
